Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P_\ell(x,\cdot)\in C^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ for each $1\le\ell\le N$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, the oscillator state consists of $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a selected causal zero-past branch, choose an onset $\tau\in I$ and require $E(x,t)=0$ and $P_\ell(x,t)=\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)=0$ for every $t\in I$ with $t\le\tau$. Continuity gives $E(x,\tau)=0$, and the equation gives $\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,\tau)=0$, consistent with the $C^2$ zero extension through onset. For $t\ge\tau$ this branch is the retarded initial-value equation with those data, so its value at time $t$ uses the applied field only on $[\tau,t]$. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; in particular, this is not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

In that frame, let $E,P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric field and polarization, and let $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a free-carrier current density. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P(x,\cdot),V(x,\cdot)\in C^1(I;\mathbb R^3)$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is V m$^{-1}$, $P$ is C m$^{-2}$, and $V$ is A m$^{-2}$. Adopt

The constant scalar parameters satisfy $\varepsilon_\infty>0$, $\mu>0$, $a>0$ and $\gamma\ge0$. Their units are respectively F m$^{-1}$, H m$^{-1}$, F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ and s$^{-1}$. The fields $V$ and $P$ have units A m$^{-2}$ and C m$^{-2}$. All coefficients are independent of $x$ and $t$, and the equation at $x$ depends only on the state and electric field at $x$; these clauses define the homogeneous, linear, spatially local closure used here. To identify these constitutive quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+P$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+P$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification within the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, $P(x,t_0)$ and $V(x,t_0)$ are state data. A constant polarization offset is fixed with the Gauss-law data and is not determined by the current equation alone. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in the laboratory frame. Its boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$ has the outward unit normal $n$ on the relative interior of each planar face; edge and vertex values will be irrelevant under the face-area convention below. Use the SI conventions of this framework. In particular $E$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $H$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $D$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, $B$ has units $\mathrm T$, and a volume current density $J$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.

For the boundary integrals, let $\mathcal F$ be the finite family of relative interiors of the planar two-dimensional faces of $\Gamma$. Write $\lambda_2$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$, defined as the restriction of Lebesgue outer measure to its Carath\'eodory-measurable sets; under the assumed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, this is a complete measure. For each face $F\in\mathcal F$, let $P_F$ be its supporting plane and fix a Euclidean isometry $\iota_F:\mathbb R^2\to P_F$. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\Gamma$ (a set in the sigma-algebra generated by the open subsets of $\Gamma$), define $dS_F(A):=\lambda_2\bigl(\iota_F^{-1}(A\cap F)\bigr)$. Any two choices of $\iota_F$ differ by an affine Euclidean isometry of $\mathbb R^2$ with absolute Jacobian determinant $1$, so the Borel change-of-variables formula makes $dS_F$ independent of that choice. Each face is bounded and lies in a finite rectangle in its plane, so $dS_F(F)<\infty$. Set $dS:=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}dS_F$ on $\Gamma$. The edges and vertices have $dS$-measure zero and are omitted, so $n$ is the outward face normal $dS$-almost everywhere; its values on edges and vertices do not affect any boundary expression. Since $dS$ is finite and Lebesgue measure restricted to $I$ is sigma-finite, $dS\otimes d\lambda_1|_I$ is the unique sigma-finite product measure on $\Gamma\times I$, with rectangle values $dS(A)\lambda_1(J)$ for Borel $A\subseteq\Gamma$ and Lebesgue-measurable $J\subseteq I$. All boundary $L^p(\Gamma)$ and $L^p(\Gamma\times I)$ spaces and almost-everywhere statements use these measures.

Every cross product in the boundary formulas is the right-handed Euclidean cross product in the positively oriented orthonormal frame basis: for $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$, as in the cross-product definition of this library.

For a real vector field $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the distribution defined by

$$\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$

As in the real graph space definition of the imported mathematical library, $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ consists of the $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with norm

$$\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by that imported weak-derivative convention. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be measurable, essentially bounded, real symmetric coefficient fields, independent of time. Require constants $0<a_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon<\infty$ and $0<a_\mu\le b_\mu<\infty$ such that, for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2.$$

The coefficient units are $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. They define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$. Define $D(t)=\varepsilon E(t)$ and $B(t)=\mu H(t)$. The spatially varying coefficient fields are explicit local model data; they are not inferred from the homogeneous material-closure postulate. Its constant symmetric branch is a special case.

A field $E:I\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is in $C^1(I;L^2)$ when it has a derivative in the $L^2$ norm at every $t\in I$ and that derivative is norm-continuous. $C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$ means norm-continuity into the graph space. A finite-energy model solution is a pair

$$E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)),$$

with $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, satisfying the adopted evolution equations as $L^2$ identities for each $t\in I$,

$$\varepsilon\,\partial_t E=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad \mu\,\partial_t H=-\operatorname{curl}E.$$

Its stored field energy is the finite real number

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E(x,t)\cdot\varepsilon(x)E(x,t)+H(x,t)\cdot\mu(x)H(x,t)\bigr)\,d\lambda_3(x).$$

There are two alternative boundary models.

**PEC.** Perfect electric conductor means $E(t)\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ for every $t$, where $H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is exactly the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ in the displayed graph norm. This closure definition is used; it is not replaced by an unproved identification with every possible trace kernel.

**Impedance.** A Green-compatible tangential boundary pair consists of measurable fields $E_\tau,H_\tau\in L^2(\Gamma\times I;\mathbb R^3)$ with $n\cdot E_\tau=n\cdot H_\tau=0$ almost everywhere and, for almost every $t$,

$$\int_\Omega\bigl(\operatorname{curl}H\cdot E-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E\bigr)\,d\lambda_3=-\int_\Gamma n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)\,dS.$$

This Green identity is part of impedance admissibility; membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ alone does not assert that such an $L^2$ pair exists. Let $Y\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ be a time-independent scalar surface admittance, in siemens, with $Y\ge0$ almost everywhere. The impedance law is

$$H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Gamma\times I.$$

Then $Y|E_\tau|^2\in L^1(\Gamma\times I)$ and is the nonnegative outward boundary-power density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. No pointwise boundary trace of an arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ field is asserted.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$. Then $F\times G$ is $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(F\times G)=\langle\operatorname{curl}F,G\rangle-\langle F,\operatorname{curl}G\rangle,$$

$$\operatorname{curl}(F\times G)=(\operatorname{div}G)F-(\operatorname{div}F)G+DF\,G-DG\,F.$$

Here $DF\,G$ denotes the map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ whose $i$th coordinate at $p$ is $\sum_{j<3}\partial_jF_i(p)\,G_j(p)$, that is, the Jacobian matrix of $F$ at $p$ applied to the vector $G(p)$, and $DG\,F$ is defined the same way with the roles of $F$ and $G$ exchanged. Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P_\ell(x,\cdot)\in C^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ for each $1\le\ell\le N$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, the oscillator state consists of $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a selected causal zero-past branch, choose an onset $\tau\in I$ and require $E(x,t)=0$ and $P_\ell(x,t)=\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)=0$ for every $t\in I$ with $t\le\tau$. Continuity gives $E(x,\tau)=0$, and the equation gives $\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,\tau)=0$, consistent with the $C^2$ zero extension through onset. For $t\ge\tau$ this branch is the retarded initial-value equation with those data, so its value at time $t$ uses the applied field only on $[\tau,t]$. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; in particular, this is not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

Assume the memory branch of the material-closure postulate [[post-em-material-closure]] in a material rest frame, and assume the hypotheses of the mathematical suppliers [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] and [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]: Countable Choice for the smooth comparison route and, in the integrable branches, Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric-field history in the material rest frame, read componentwise in its spatial basis ([[def-em-fields]]), and let $P$ be the polarisation response declared by the model.

**(a) [Causal response]** If the kernel of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) satisfies $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$, then for every bounded continuous history $E$ the response $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ is well defined for every $t$, bounded and continuous, linear in $E$, and causal: histories equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$ produce responses equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$.

**(b) [Transfer function and dispersion relations]** If $K$ is smooth with compact support in $(0,\infty)$, the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1}|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ (with the whole-plane bound carrying the exponential factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ when $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$), and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](b). If $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$, then $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, obeys the stated growth bound, and satisfies the same pair of relations; an instantaneous real part $\chi_\infty$ may be added to the model, and the relations apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty$ for $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$.

**(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches]** For each specified integer $n\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. Any transfer-only physical branch additionally requires $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ entrywise for every real $\omega$, including real $\chi(0)$, as in [[post-em-material-closure]](c); scalar transfers act as scalar matrices. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. The Taylor polynomial and residual are

$$P_n(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)}{j!}(z-\omega_0)^j,\qquad f_n(z)=\frac{\chi(z)-P_n(z)}{(z-\omega_0)^n},$$

with removable values and the boundary $C^1$ hypothesis read entrywise as in the supplier. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is included only under its own decay and boundary hypotheses: $P_0=0$, $f_0=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ with the supplier's principal-value convention. The separate constitutive-polynomial branch declares the normalized polarisation $P/\varepsilon_0=\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$, with real scalar coefficients (acting as scalar matrices) or real $3\times3$ matrices $A_j$ whose entries carry $\mathrm s^j$, and $K$ satisfying the supplier's integrable causal hypotheses, is causal on histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$. Its transfer is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, without assuming that $Q$ is the Taylor polynomial $P_n$.

**(d) [Monochromatic work, instantaneous work and passivity]** Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^3$ and $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\chi(\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\chi_\infty+\chi(\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is present. For a transfer-function-only branch adopt $P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$ as the harmonic response convention; in a kernel or normalized polynomial branch this follows by substitution. Here $e$ has units $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is dimensionless, $e^*$ denotes conjugate transpose, $(C^*)_{jk}=\overline{C_{kj}}$ for a complex matrix $C$, a matrix $H$ is Hermitian when $H^*=H$ and is positive semidefinite when $v^*Hv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^3$, in the convention of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](d), and $\langle g\rangle:=T^{-1}\int_0^Tg(t)\,dt$ with $T=2\pi/\omega$. The period-averaged work per unit volume, in $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, is

$$\langle E\cdot\partial_tP\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e).$$

It is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if the full Hermitian dissipative part

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)-\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)^*}{2i}$$

is positive semidefinite. This frequencywise monochromatic passivity is an additional model condition, not a consequence of causality or dispersion.

For the instantaneous part set $S=(\chi_\infty+\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $A=(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is

$$E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot S E\right)+\varepsilon_0 E\cdot A\partial_tE.$$

The symmetric part therefore supplies the quadratic storage term; no positivity of that term is asserted unless $S$ is additionally positive semidefinite. The antisymmetric part has $E\cdot A E=0$ but can supply nonzero work over a cycle. Its monochromatic contribution is $\varepsilon_0\omega\operatorname{Im}(e^*A e)/2$, and

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=M_K(\omega)+A/i,\qquad M_K(\omega)=\frac{\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*}{2i}.$$

Thus only a symmetric real instantaneous matrix contributes purely this storage term for all histories; for an arbitrary real instantaneous matrix the passivity test must include its antisymmetric contribution. For example, $\chi_\infty=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $K=0$ and $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ give $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$, zero quadratic storage and averaged work $\varepsilon_0\omega>0$. The opposite circular amplitude $(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$, so this instantaneous response is causal but fails the all-amplitude passivity condition.

**(e) [Scope]** The response is declared in the material rest frame of [[post-em-material-closure]](a); boosting the material changes the fields and the rest observer, and no frame-independent instantaneous response law is asserted. The framework does not claim that any particular material realises these branches, no microscopic mechanism is derived, and no empirical statement is made.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

**(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches]** For each specified integer $n\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. Any transfer-only physical branch additionally requires $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ entrywise for every real $\omega$, including real $\chi(0)$, as in [[post-em-material-closure]](c); scalar transfers act as scalar matrices. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. The Taylor polynomial and residual are

$$P_n(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)}{j!}(z-\omega_0)^j,\qquad f_n(z)=\frac{\chi(z)-P_n(z)}{(z-\omega_0)^n},$$

with removable values and the boundary $C^1$ hypothesis read entrywise as in the supplier. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is included only under its own decay and boundary hypotheses: $P_0=0$, $f_0=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ with the supplier's principal-value convention. The separate constitutive-polynomial branch declares the normalized polarisation $P/\varepsilon_0=\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$, with real scalar coefficients (acting as scalar matrices) or real $3\times3$ matrices $A_j$ whose entries carry $\mathrm s^j$, and $K$ satisfying the supplier's integrable causal hypotheses, is causal on histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$. Its transfer is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, without assuming that $Q$ is the Taylor polynomial $P_n$.

**(d) [Monochromatic work, instantaneous work and passivity]** Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^3$ and $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\chi(\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\chi_\infty+\chi(\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is present. For a transfer-function-only branch adopt $P(t)=\operatorname{Re}(\varepsilon_0\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e e^{-i\omega t})$ as the harmonic response convention; in a kernel or normalized polynomial branch this follows by substitution. Here $e$ has units $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is dimensionless, $e^*$ denotes conjugate transpose, $(C^*)_{jk}=\overline{C_{kj}}$ for a complex matrix $C$, a matrix $H$ is Hermitian when $H^*=H$ and is positive semidefinite when $v^*Hv\ge0$ for every $v\in\mathbb C^3$, in the convention of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](d), and $\langle g\rangle:=T^{-1}\int_0^Tg(t)\,dt$ with $T=2\pi/\omega$. The period-averaged work per unit volume, in $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-3}$, is

$$\langle E\cdot\partial_tP\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e).$$

It is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if the full Hermitian dissipative part

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)-\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)^*}{2i}$$

is positive semidefinite. This frequencywise monochromatic passivity is an additional model condition, not a consequence of causality or dispersion.

For the instantaneous part set $S=(\chi_\infty+\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $A=(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is

$$E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot S E\right)+\varepsilon_0 E\cdot A\partial_tE.$$

The symmetric part therefore supplies the quadratic storage term; no positivity of that term is asserted unless $S$ is additionally positive semidefinite. The antisymmetric part has $E\cdot A E=0$ but can supply nonzero work over a cycle. Its monochromatic contribution is $\varepsilon_0\omega\operatorname{Im}(e^*A e)/2$, and

$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=M_K(\omega)+A/i,\qquad M_K(\omega)=\frac{\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*}{2i}.$$

Thus only a symmetric real instantaneous matrix contributes purely this storage term for all histories; for an arbitrary real instantaneous matrix the passivity test must include its antisymmetric contribution. For example, $\chi_\infty=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $K=0$ and $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ give $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$, zero quadratic storage and averaged work $\varepsilon_0\omega>0$. The opposite circular amplitude $(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$, so this instantaneous response is causal but fails the all-amplitude passivity condition.

**(e) [Scope]** The response is declared in the material rest frame of [[post-em-material-closure]](a); boosting the material changes the fields and the rest observer, and no frame-independent instantaneous response law is asserted. The framework does not claim that any particular material realises these branches, no microscopic mechanism is derived, and no empirical statement is made.

$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$

The complex exponential is entire, and

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Suppose

and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
(A continuous function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable, by Heine-Cantor and Riemann's criterion).

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and

   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

derivations.claim: For a real harmonic history $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$, complexify the real linear ODE [A1] by extending its real coefficients complex-linearly and use the ansatz $\widetilde P_\ell(t)=p_\ell e^{-i\omega t}$. By the derivative of the complex exponential and the chain rule, one and two time derivatives multiply the amplitude by $-i\omega$ and $-\omega^2$, respectively, so the complex amplitude equation is $(\omega_\ell^2-\omega^2-i\gamma_\ell\omega)p_\ell=a_\ell e$. Its real part is a real harmonic particular solution of [A1]. Wherever this scalar denominator is nonzero, the amplitude is uniquely $p_\ell=\frac{a_\ell}{\omega_\ell^2-\omega^2-i\gamma_\ell\omega}e$, including when $e=0$. Summing gives the stated harmonic particular-solution multiplier without dividing by the vector amplitude. This does not identify the undamped coefficient with a retarded zero-past response.

The roots of $\omega_\ell^2-z^2-i\gamma_\ell z=0$ are $z=-i\gamma_\ell/2\pm\sqrt{\omega_\ell^2-\gamma_\ell^2/4}$. If $0\le\gamma_\ell<2\omega_\ell$, the square root is real and both roots have imaginary part $-\gamma_\ell/2\le0$; at $\gamma_\ell=0$ they are the real values $\pm\omega_\ell$. If $\gamma_\ell=2\omega_\ell$, the repeated root is $-i\omega_\ell$. If $\gamma_\ell>2\omega_\ell$, write $\beta=\sqrt{\gamma_\ell^2/4-\omega_\ell^2}$; then $0<\beta<\gamma_\ell/2$ and the roots $-i(\gamma_\ell/2\mp\beta)$ both have strictly negative imaginary part. Hence no denominator vanishes in the open upper half-plane, proving analyticity there; the undamped real poles are exactly the stated boundary exceptions.

Fix one oscillator, denote its parameters by $a,\omega_0,\gamma$, assume $\gamma>0$, and set $g(t)=0$ for $t<0$. For $t\ge0$, define the retarded kernel by $g(t)=e^{-\gamma t/2}\sin(\alpha t)/\alpha$ if $0<\gamma<2\omega_0$, $g(t)=te^{-\omega_0t}$ if $\gamma=2\omega_0$, and $g(t)=\bigl(e^{-(\gamma/2-\beta)t}-e^{-(\gamma/2+\beta)t}\bigr)/(2\beta)$ if $\gamma>2\omega_0$, where $\alpha=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2/4}$ and $\beta=\sqrt{\gamma^2/4-\omega_0^2}$ in their respective cases. Differentiating with [F2] gives $g(0)=0$, $g'(0+)=1$ and $g''+\gamma g'+\omega_0^2g=0$ for $t>0$. The underdamped $g,g'$ decay at rate $\gamma/2$; the critical formula and derivative are bounded by $Ce^{-\omega_0t/2}$; the overdamped formula and derivative are bounded by $Ce^{-(\gamma/2-\beta)t}$, with $\gamma/2-\beta>0$. Hence $g,g'\in L^1(0,\infty)$. For each positive decay rate $\lambda$, $te^{-\lambda t}$ is integrable by integration by parts on $[0,T]$ and [F3] as $T\to\infty$, so also $tg\in L^1(0,\infty)$.

For each real vector history $E\in C^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$ with $E,E',E''$ bounded, set $P(t)=a\int_0^\infty g(s)E(t-s)\,ds$. Apply [F4] componentwise: the derivative integrands are measurable and bounded, uniformly in $t$, by $\|E'\|_\infty|g|$ and $\|E''\|_\infty|g|$, which are integrable by step 1.3. Thus $P_{tt}+\gamma P_t+\omega_0^2P=a\int_0^\infty[g(s)E''(t-s)+\gamma g(s)E'(t-s)+\omega_0^2g(s)E(t-s)]\,ds$.

For real $\omega>0$, put $A_\ell=\omega_\ell^2-\omega^2$ and $B_\ell=\gamma_\ell\omega$. Away from an undamped pole, $A_\ell-iB_\ell\ne0$ and $\frac{a_\ell}{A_\ell-iB_\ell}=\frac{a_\ell(A_\ell+iB_\ell)}{A_\ell^2+B_\ell^2}$, so $\operatorname{Im}(a_\ell/(A_\ell-iB_\ell))=a_\ell\gamma_\ell\omega/(A_\ell^2+\gamma_\ell^2\omega^2)\ge0$. Since $\varepsilon_\infty$ is real, summing these expressions proves the displayed nonnegative imaginary part of $\varepsilon$. At $\gamma_\ell=0$ and $\omega=\omega_\ell$ the denominator vanishes, so this pointwise computation and pointwise formula do not apply.

Integrating by parts twice on $[0,T]$ and taking $T\to\infty$ is valid because $g,g'$ decay by step 1.3, $g''=-\gamma g'-\omega_0^2g\in L^1$, and $E,E'$ are bounded. The boundary values $g(0)=0$, $g'(0+)=1$ give $\int_0^\infty g(s)E''(t-s)\,ds=E(t)+\int_0^\infty g''(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ and $\int_0^\infty g(s)E'(t-s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty g'(s)E(t-s)\,ds$. Substitution in step 2.1 cancels the integral by $g''+\gamma g'+\omega_0^2g=0$, leaving $P_{tt}+\gamma P_t+\omega_0^2P=aE$.

The normalized kernel $K=(a/\varepsilon_0)g$ is real, causal and locally absolutely continuous; step 1.3 gives $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$. For $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, exponential decay makes the boundary terms vanish in integration by parts, so $\int_0^\infty g'(s)e^{izs}ds=-izG(z)$ and $\int_0^\infty g''(s)e^{izs}ds=-1-z^2G(z)$, where $G(z)=\int_0^\infty g(s)e^{izs}ds$. The Green equation gives $(\omega_0^2-z^2-i\gamma z)G(z)=1$, hence the normalized transfer is $(a/\varepsilon_0)/(\omega_0^2-z^2-i\gamma z)$. Summing the finite kernels gives $\chi_{\mathrm{norm}}=\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}/\varepsilon_0$; with [F1], this kernel satisfies every hypothesis of [L1], which yields causality, upper-half-plane analyticity and the unsubtracted Hilbert relations for the strictly damped branch. Multiplication by $\varepsilon_0$ gives the same relations for $\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty=\chi_{\mathrm{abs}}$.

Use a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. In that frame, let $E,P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric field and polarization, and let $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a free-carrier current density. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P(x,\cdot),V(x,\cdot)\in C^1(I;\mathbb R^3)$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is V m$^{-1}$, $P$ is C m$^{-2}$, and $V$ is A m$^{-2}$. Adopt

$$\partial_tP(x,t)=V(x,t),\qquad \partial_tV(x,t)+\gamma V(x,t)=aE(x,t),$$

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+P(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t).$$

The constant scalar parameters satisfy $\varepsilon_\infty>0$, $\mu>0$, $a>0$ and $\gamma\ge0$. Their units are respectively F m$^{-1}$, H m$^{-1}$, F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$ and s$^{-1}$. The fields $V$ and $P$ have units A m$^{-2}$ and C m$^{-2}$. All coefficients are independent of $x$ and $t$, and the equation at $x$ depends only on the state and electric field at $x$; these clauses define the homogeneous, linear, spatially local closure used here. To identify these constitutive quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+P$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+P$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification within the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, $P(x,t_0)$ and $V(x,t_0)$ are state data. A constant polarization offset is fixed with the Gauss-law data and is not determined by the current equation alone. The branch $\gamma=0$ is the collisionless model; it has no decaying stationary impulse kernel, and its zero-frequency response is not part of this postulate. This is a phenomenological closure, not a derivation of carrier mass, density, collision statistics or any actual material response.

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

**(a) [Bound-source conservation]** $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then

$$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$

as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.

**(b) [Macroscopic equations]** On $\Omega\times I$,

$$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

$$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$

for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ with entries in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]) and units $\mathrm s^{-1}$; the integral then converges absolutely because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a dimensionless scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]). $$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in one material rest frame. Use real SI fields: $E,H,D,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, a free current density $J_f:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization $P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and, when present, carrier current $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$. Their units are V m$^{-1}$, A m$^{-1}$, C m$^{-2}$, T, A m$^{-2}$, C m$^{-2}$ and A m$^{-2}$, respectively. Let $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ and $\mu>0$ be constant scalar coefficients in F m$^{-1}$ and H m$^{-1}$. Each $u_L,u_D$ is in J m$^{-3}$ and the flux $E\times H$ is in W m$^{-2}$.

Assume Countable Choice, the smooth macroscopic Maxwell material model, and its curl equations

$$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$$

hold pointwise. The smooth macroscopic material model includes continuous free sources and the total polarization/magnetization identifications specified by the Lorentz or Drude closure. Assume $E,H$ are jointly $C^\infty$ pointwise and satisfy $E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$; $J_f$ and each material-current term belong to $C(I;L^2)$. Here $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is the real $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with the graph norm. Take Lorentz fields $P_\ell$ jointly $C^\infty$ and in $C^2(I;L^2)$, or Drude fields $P,V$ jointly $C^\infty$ with $V\in C^1(I;L^2)$, so that the stored energies and current terms are finite. Take either one of the following constitutive branches:

1. **Finite Lorentz branch.** For some finite $N\ge1$, $D=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell$, $B=\mu H$, and
   $$\partial_t^2P_\ell+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell=a_\ell E,$$
   where $P_\ell$ is jointly $C^2$, $a_\ell>0$ in F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ in s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ in s$^{-1}$.
2. **Drude branch.** $D=\varepsilon_\infty E+P$, $B=\mu H$, $\partial_tP=V$, and $\partial_tV+\gamma V=aE$, where $P,V$ are jointly $C^1$, $a>0$ in F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, and $\gamma\ge0$ in s$^{-1}$.

For the Lorentz branch define

$$u_L:=\frac{\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2}{2}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2}{2a_\ell}.$$

For the Drude branch define

$$u_D:=\frac{\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2}{2}+\frac{|V|^2}{2a}.$$

The Lorentz density is positive definite in $(E,H,(P_\ell,\partial_tP_\ell)_{\ell=1}^N)$. The Drude density is positive definite in $(E,H,V)$; a constant polarization offset is not part of this energy.

Then the respective local identities hold pointwise:

$$\partial_tu_L+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-E\cdot J_f-\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{\gamma_\ell}{a_\ell}|\partial_tP_\ell|^2,$$

$$\partial_tu_D+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-E\cdot J_f-\frac{\gamma}{a}|V|^2.$$

If, in addition, the fields satisfy the exact closure-defined PEC branch of the finite-energy boundary model and $J_f=0$, then the total stored energy $U(t)=\int_\Omega u_L(x,t)\,dx$ or $U(t)=\int_\Omega u_D(x,t)\,dx$ is nonnegative and nonincreasing. More generally the corresponding fixed-volume balance includes the work $-\int E\cdot J_f$ and the displayed nonnegative material-loss terms; no claim of conservation without these terms is made.
